idiom_name: Enumerator::Lazy chain (#lazy) forced by a terminal call
implementation_notes: Ruby ships the lazy form as Enumerator::Lazy: calling #lazy on an Enumerable gives an enumerator that allows constructing chains of operations without evaluating them immediately, evaluating values on an as-needed basis, and it redefines most Enumerable methods so each call returns another lazy enumerator. A chain such as .lazy.select { }.map { }.take(100) therefore performs one pass over the source and works over infinite enumerators; the chain stays unevaluated until a terminal method (.to_a, .force, .first, .sum, .each) asks for values. Without #lazy the same methods build a new Array per stage.
code_sketch:
total = people.lazy
  .select { |p| p.age > 18 }      # Enumerator::Lazy
  .map { |p| p.score }
  .take(100)
  .sum                            # terminal: single pass
# infinite: (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy.map { |i| i * i }.first(5)
pitfalls: Forgetting #lazy is invisible: Array#map/#select allocate a new array per stage, so the pipeline silently keeps every intermediate.
Lazy chains are not memoized: reusing an Enumerator::Lazy in two places re-evaluates it (and re-reads its source) on every traversal.
Per-element blocks plus a proxy object per stage cost more than a hand-written each loop for short chains; #lazy pays off with large, infinite or expensive sources.
